title: Ten days away
note: Fictional patient. Values are illustrative; the prescription, its efficiency, and any urgent-treatment orders are the attending nephrologist’s.
intro: You are the physician on duty. Mr. Rogelio Santos, 54, has been on hemodialysis for two years. He missed ten days while caring for his father in the province. This morning his BUN is 232 mg/dL, potassium 6.4 mmol/L with tall T waves, and bicarbonate 13 mmol/L. The nurse has set up his usual maintenance order: four hours, full blood flow.

choices.text: Start the unit’s hyperkalemia order set and keep him on a monitor; call the attending nephrologist with SBAR: a very high urea after missed sessions puts him at risk of disequilibrium, so the usual order may not fit; ask for a written order for today and repeat it back.
choices.feedback: He needs dialysis today for his potassium, but a patient returning after missed sessions with a very high urea is at risk of disequilibrium. Prevention belongs to the order; when the order and the patient do not match, you call.
choices.then: The attending orders a shorter, gentler first session today, with another tomorrow.

choices.text: Run the usual four hours at full flow: his potassium needs it.
choices.feedback: Potassium is a reason to dialyze, not a reason for a full-efficiency session after ten days away. A large urea drop in one session is the pattern that produces disequilibrium.
choices.then: The nurse asks you to confirm with the attending, who orders a gentler session.

choices.text: Shorten the session to two hours yourself.
choices.feedback: Your instinct is right, but you do not change the order. Call the attending, who sets the prescription.
choices.then: You call the attending, who writes the order.

n2.scene: At 1 hour 25 minutes he has a pounding headache, nausea, and cannot settle in the chair.

choices.text: Go to the chair; ask the nurse to slow or stop the treatment per protocol; check glucose, blood pressure, pulse, and a brief neurologic examination; call the attending.
choices.feedback: In a patient after missed sessions, a headache is disequilibrium until you have checked the pressure, the sugar, and the nervous system and called the attending. Treatment once the syndrome is established rarely works, so early recognition matters.

vitals.neuro: Oriented; pupils equal; moves all limbs

choices.feedback: That treats the symptom while the cause, if it is disequilibrium, keeps running. Slow or stop and check.
choices.then: Twenty minutes later he vomits and is drowsier. You go to the chair and ask the nurse to stop.

vitals.neuro: Drowsy; pupils equal; moves all limbs

choices.text: Increase the blood flow to finish the session sooner.
choices.feedback: Faster clearance is exactly what drives disequilibrium.
choices.then: The nurse refuses and slows the treatment. You go to the chair.

n3.scene: Glucose 104 mg/dL. Blood pressure 188/100. He is oriented, pupils equal, moving all limbs, speech normal. He received heparin at the start.
n3.prompt: What do you report to the attending?

choices.text: Time into the session, blood flow, the symptoms and when they began, glucose, pressure, the neurologic findings, and the heparin given; ask whether to end the session.
choices.feedback: Disequilibrium is a diagnosis of exclusion. High pressure, low sugar, and bleeding inside the skull (more likely after heparin) all look similar. The attending needs all of it to decide.

choices.text: “He has a headache; I think it is disequilibrium.”
choices.feedback: Give the findings, not only your conclusion, including the heparin, which matters if bleeding is possible.

choices.text: Nothing yet; see if it settles first.
choices.feedback: Stop and call. Symptoms in a patient after missed sessions go to the attending at once.

n4.scene: The session ended early. His post-dialysis BUN is 165 mg/dL. A nurse says, “That’s a URR of under 30%. He’s underdialyzed; let’s add an hour.”

choices.text: (232 − 165) ÷ 232 = about 29%: that is what a deliberately gentle session aims for. Maintenance targets do not apply today. The attending plans frequent short sessions over the next days.
choices.feedback: A low URR is expected in a deliberately gentle first session; it does not mean the dose was inadequate. Urea is lowered in stages.
Adding an hour now repeats the risk you just stopped. The plan is more sessions, not a longer one today.

choices.text: Leave it to the attending to decide.
choices.feedback: The attending decides, but you should know why a low URR is intended today and say so.

n5.scene: Before he leaves, Mr. Santos says he may need to go back to the province next week.

choices.text: Document the reason for the missed sessions, refer him to the social worker for transient dialysis near his father, and make sure his next sessions are booked and he knows the warning signs.
choices.feedback: Missed sessions have reasons. Here the fix is practical: dialysis near his father, arranged through the transient-dialysis process.

choices.text: Warn him that missing dialysis could kill him.
choices.feedback: He knows. A lecture will not solve the problem of caring for his father; a plan will.
Record it, but act on it: a referral and a plan for transient dialysis.

end.title: The week after
end.text: Two more short sessions brought his urea down in stages without further symptoms. The social worker arranged transient dialysis at a unit near his father’s town. Your record shows the time of onset, your findings, each step, and the advice received.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • A very high urea after missed sessions carries disequilibrium risk; prevention is in the order.
  • When the order and the patient do not match, call; do not change it yourself.
  • New headache: slow or stop, check pressure, sugar, and neurology, and call.
  • A low URR in a gentle session is intended.
  • Find the reason for missed sessions, and solve it.

See Disequilibrium and Preventing and recognizing it.
